title: How Democrats Won the 2026 Midterms
author: Youth Outsider Editorial Team
dek: A war that ran long, gas that cost more, a president who asked to be on the ballot, and a slate of candidates who didn't look like the usual Democrats. Here is how the party turned an expected wave into a rout.
cover_alt: Collage of Democratic winners in front of a map of the states Democrats flipped in 2026
cover_caption: Collage by Youth Outsider. Map: U.S. Census Bureau boundaries. Photo credits pending.
body:
All the signs pointed toward a good night for Democrats on Tuesday. Almost nobody predicted this one.

Democrats won the House and the Senate, flipping seven Senate seats on their way to a 54-seat majority, with races in Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled, [according to NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/senate-results). They took the governor's offices in Georgia, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada. Texas is sending a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since 1988, and Kansas for the [first time since 1932](https://www.kcur.org/politics-elections-and-government/2026-11-03/hamilton-wins-kansans-elect-democratic-senator-for-the-first-time-in-nearly-a-century). Pre-election polls had Democrats ahead by about eight points on the national generic ballot. The final voter survey suggests the real margin was [at least 13](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-6022216/midterms-democrats-trump-republicans-analysis).

NPR's Domenico Montanaro compared the night to 2006, the last time Democrats took back both chambers at once, in the middle of an unpopular war. The comparison fits. But no single issue explains a result this big. Four things came together.

## 1. The war

On Feb. 28, the United States went to war with Iran. The White House said the operation would take [four to six weeks](https://www.dailysignal.com/2026/11/04/iran-war-plays-major-role-in-midterm-blowout/). By Election Day it had lasted eight months, with a shaky ceasefire, a U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and repeated attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

Voters made the connection. In NBC's exit poll, 74% said the Iran war was a crucial factor in their vote, and those voters backed Democrats 62% to 35%. In CBS's exit poll, most voters said the decision to take military action was a mistake, including about a quarter of Republicans. Trump's approval, which stood at 48% before the war, fell as low as [36% in the polling average](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-6022216/midterms-democrats-trump-republicans-analysis).

Even the president acknowledged it. *"I think a part of it was Iran,"* Trump told Fox Business the day after the election. People agreed with his Iran policy, he argued, but "weren't willing to do the short-term consequence" of paying more for gas.

A second foreign policy fight played out mostly inside the Democratic Party. A Gallup survey in February found that Americans' sympathies leaned toward the Palestinians over the Israelis, 41% to 36%, the [first time in 25 years](https://www.npr.org/2026/07/31/nx-s1-5896216/democrats-israel-congress-2026-midterm-elections) that had happened, with the biggest shifts among Democrats and younger voters. In July, 103 House Democrats voted to cut $3.3 billion in aid to Israel. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, who called the war in Gaza a genocide and opposed military aid to Israel, beat an AIPAC-backed opponent in the primary and then won the general election by about seven points. Gaza did not decide the national result the way Iran did, but it shaped who Democrats nominated and helped keep young, progressive voters engaged.

## 2. Prices

The war came home at the gas pump. By early May, the national average for a gallon of regular hit $4.54, the [highest since July 2022](https://abc7ny.com/post/average-us-gas-prices-top-450-gallon-highest-4-years/19050172/) and $1.54 more than before the war began, according to GasBuddy. Diesel rose with it, pushing up the cost of moving everything else.

That landed on voters who were already stretched. In NBC's exit poll, 39% named the economy as the most important issue, and 75% said the national economy was in poor shape. About two-thirds said Trump's policies had made things worse, and more than 60% [held him responsible for high prices](https://www.dailysignal.com/2026/11/04/iran-war-plays-major-role-in-midterm-blowout/). The worries were concrete: 88% were concerned about grocery prices, 87% about gas and diesel, 86% about utilities and 85% about health care.

Democrats built their campaigns around that list. Talarico ran on costs and corruption. Gina Hinojosa promised to send every Texas household $1,500 from the state's savings. In Georgia, Ossoff tied his opponent to tariffs, Medicaid cuts and the price of fuel. Republicans tried to change the subject. *"Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater,"* Vice President JD Vance told a Republican gathering in Dallas, asking voters to look past the prices to the bigger picture. Most didn't.

The economy also helps explain the night's biggest demographic swing. Latino voters, who moved toward Trump in 2024 largely because of inflation, [moved back hard](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-6022216/midterms-democrats-trump-republicans-analysis). Prices didn't come down, and aggressive deportation tactics angered many of them: 68% of Hispanic voters disapproved of how ICE was doing its job. In South Texas, districts Republicans had redrawn to win ended up competitive instead.

## 3. Trump himself

Midterms are usually a referendum on the president. Trump made sure this one was. In a 32-day campaign blitz, he told supporters to *"pretend I'm on the ballot."* They did. In CBS's exit poll, 59% said the president was a factor in their House vote. Sixty-two percent disapproved of the job he was doing, according to the AP's voter survey, and three-quarters of voters said they were angry or dissatisfied with the direction of the country.

The slide was steep. Before the Iran war, Trump's approval stood at 48% in the polling average. By the fall it had fallen as low as 36%, [according to NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-6022216/midterms-democrats-trump-republicans-analysis). Some of that was the war and the prices that came with it. But some of it was about Trump himself. In the AP survey, 62% said he puts his own interests ahead of the country's, and NPR reported that corruption rose as an issue in the final months of the campaign.

The Jeffrey Epstein files were part of that story. Trump had promised supporters that the files would come out, then resisted their release for months. Even before this year, a [Reuters/Ipsos poll](https://www.dailywire.com/news/more-than-two-thirds-of-americans-believe-government-is-hiding-details-on-epstein-case-poll) found that 69% of Americans believed the government was hiding details about Epstein's clients, including about two-thirds of Republicans, and only 17% approved of how Trump was handling the case. Democrats returned to the issue all year, and it was one of the few that split Trump's own base.

So did his style. Trump picked personal fights with the candidates running against his party, and the fights often helped them. In August, after Jon Ossoff mocked him at an Atlanta rally, Trump called the Georgia senator a "Pee-wee Herman look-alike," and a White House spokesman called Ossoff a "cringeworthy, feminine theatre kid cosplaying as Barack Obama." The exchange gave a Democrat in a Trump state a week of national attention. Trump also went after the faith of two Democrats who were running on it. He attacked Talarico over a 2021 podcast in which the Texan called himself a "Christian who hates Christianity," and said Kansas's Adam Hamilton "openly mocks Jesus," [according to The Christian Post](https://www.christianpost.com/news/10-christian-democrats-seeking-election-on-nov-3.html). Both men won.

His personal involvement didn't move votes the way Republicans hoped. Trump and Vance each visited Kansas twice to rally for Sen. Roger Marshall. Hamilton's lead in Emerson's polling [grew after the visits](https://www.kcur.org/politics-elections-and-government/2026-11-03/hamilton-wins-kansans-elect-democratic-senator-for-the-first-time-in-nearly-a-century). Trump also pushed Republican-led states to redraw their congressional maps to add GOP seats. In South Texas, that backfired: spreading Republican voters across more districts left several of them competitive, and NPR called the result a textbook "dummymander."

After the results came in, he did not take the blame. *"They didn't like the candidates, and some of the candidates that I endorsed fought me,"* he told Fox Business. Asked about Iran, he said, *"Haven't finished the job, and maybe I will, and maybe I won't."* Just before midnight on election night, he posted an image of a red hat with one word on it: "VETO." With Democrats about to take over both chambers of Congress, it was an early sign of the standoff ahead.

## 4. The candidates

Anger at the party in power creates an opening. Somebody still has to win the seat. This year Democrats ran an unusual group of candidates, many of whom didn't fit the national image of the party, in places where that image is toxic.

The most striking were two men of faith. James Talarico, a 37-year-old former middle school teacher and Presbyterian seminarian, talked about Christianity more than almost any Democrat in national politics and beat Attorney General Ken Paxton by about 12 points, despite Republicans spending more than $413 million on the race. In Kansas, the Rev. Adam Hamilton, who leads the Church of the Resurrection, the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, ran as an "independent-minded Democrat" promising "decency." He beat Sen. Roger Marshall after Trump and Vance each visited the state twice to campaign against him. *"We are better together, Republicans and Democrats,"* Hamilton told supporters on Tuesday night.

They weren't the only nontraditional picks. In Iowa, Josh Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medalist in wheelchair basketball who called himself a "prairie populist," flipped a seat Republicans had held for more than a decade. In Maine, Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger, replaced the party's original nominee with about 100 days to go and ended Susan Collins's bid for a sixth term. In South Carolina, Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, beat Darline Graham, who had been appointed to her late brother Lindsey Graham's seat.

Democrats also landed the kind of recruits party leaders spend whole cycles chasing: proven statewide winners who had already shown they could carry red and purple states. In North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper, who won the governorship twice in a state Trump carried all three times, beat Republican Michael Whatley 59% to 39%, a nearly 20-point margin for the state's open Senate seat. In Ohio, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his seat in 2024, came back to beat Sen. Jon Husted in a special election by about five points, [according to NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/senate-results). And in Alaska, former Rep. Mary Peltola, the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, held a narrow lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan, 48.2% to 47.9%, with about three-quarters of the vote counted and the race still too close to call. Recruits like these gave Democrats candidates voters already knew and trusted, which made it harder for Republicans to tie them to the national party.

What many of these candidates shared was an ability to talk to voters who don't usually vote for Democrats, about faith, about work, about costs, without sounding like they were reading from a national script.

## What comes next

Democrats should be careful about what they read into Tuesday. The party is not suddenly popular. In the AP's voter survey, Republicans had a 41% favorable rating, and Democrats were only somewhat better at 47%. Many voters were voting against the president more than for anyone. With a narrow Senate majority, no filibuster-proof margin and a president promising vetoes, Democrats will struggle to deliver the relief they promised.

The bigger question is 2028. Democrats proved they can win in Texas, Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina. They did it with an unpopular war and $4.50 gas as tailwinds, and with a president who wanted the election to be about him. Next time, Trump won't be on the ballot, even in spirit. Whether the coalition that showed up on Tuesday shows up again without him is the question both parties will spend the next two years trying to answer.
